segments.text: You're listening to the political scene. I'm David Remnick.
Early each week, we bring you a conversation from our episode of The New Yorker Radio Hour.
The New Yorker Radio Hour is a co-production of WNYC and The New Yorker.
Welcome to The New Yorker Radio Hour. I'm David Remnick.
Conventional wisdom in politics, well, it can turn on a dime, as we've just seen.
Weeks ago on this program, we were raising serious questions about whether free and fair midterm elections would even take place.
take place. Now, call it a tsunami, call it an earthquake, what have you, the Democrats
will hold large majorities in the House of Representatives and the Senate.
Maybe most shocking of all, the president skipped right over denial and immediately
began finger pointing at his allies, something and someone to blame for the defeat.
Our guest today, Pete Buttigieg, is no stranger to quick turns in politics. In a few months
of 2019, he went from running a small Indiana city, South Bend, to emerging as a plausible
candidate for the presidency. And while he came up short, his star did not dim. He joined
the Biden administration, and this year he's been one of the most in-demand Democratic
surrogates on the campaign trail. Buttigieg is widely expected to be a candidate once
again in 2028.
But two years can be a very long time, as we've seen. If the Democrats are going to
hold on to victory long enough to elect a president, then they'll have to figure out
how to make an impact in these next two years, even with an angry lame duck in the White
House.
I asked Pete Buttigieg what that might look like.
We're speaking now after a momentous election.
Tell me how you're feeling and maybe more deeply, what does this all mean?
Well, it's extraordinary.
And I think it is the beginning of a change in the era that we're living in.
Now a lot depends on what happens next.
This is more of an opening than it is an answer.
But I think fundamentally there was a widespread
and wholesale rejection of Donald Trump's policies
on the congressional Republicans who enabled him.
The American people clearly saw corruption
and their economic frustrations
as two categories of things that were related to each other.
They voted accordingly.
The president invited the electorate
to imagine that he was on the ballot.
I think what happened is we took him up on that.
That's why there was such just a resounding, extraordinary defeat for the Republicans,
frankly, beyond anything that I really hoped could happen, even though I was working hard
to do my best to help make it happen.
I think it's fair to say that the Democratic Party's brand as such did not exactly get
soaring ratings.
Is there a possibility that you interpret or that this election can be overinterpreted
as an endorsement of the Democratic Party rather than a repudiation of Donald Trump
and MAGA specifically?
Yeah, that's part of what I mean when I say this is an opening rather than a solution.
What has happened is Democrats have been given a chance.
This doesn't mean everybody suddenly fell in love with the Democratic Party.
What it means is that Democratic candidates, sometimes as part of the party, sometimes
in spite of the party label, persuaded voters that we had better answers.
And I do think one thing that's important to recognize is, you know, for years now,
it has been the case that democratic policies have been more popular than the democratic party
or democratic politicians.
And by the way, this is new.
When I came of age, our position on taxing the wealthy, for example, was not as popular as it was now.
Our position on healthcare certainly is much more popular now than it used to be.
A whole bunch of things we used to be on defense around are now things people believe, but we still weren't winning elections.
So I think the best thing that could happen is for our brand and our politicians to come in line with our policy commitments.
The most important ones that really unite about two-thirds of the country and pretty much a hundred percent of the party.
If we stick to those in the new congressional majorities and state trifectas that have been created,
Then I think there's an enormous opportunity to change what people assume and what people
picture when they picture the Democratic Party.
Now, this isn't the first time people have declared the Trump era over.
I can, with some abashments say that the New Yorker had a headline eight years ago on a
piece online that said, in essence, you know, this is the end of the Trump era or it's
about to end.
I forget which flagrant piece of misbehavior it was commenting on.
I think we can agree that was premature. Are you ready to declare the fever broken now?
Look, we thought the fever was broken around January 6th and many other times.
This was the Trump era, even when he was out of power. And right now,
he's in power, at least he's in power in the White House. So I do think it's way too soon to say the
era has come to an end. You felt that acutely while you were in the Biden administration that you
were still living in the Trump era? When you look back on it. I think in retrospect, you can see it.
Yeah, even when we were in charge, it was kind of his world and we were living in it.
I would really say ever since he came down that escalator 10 or 11 years ago, that's been the
case. I think he represented a middle finger to the status quo, and people were outraged at the
way things worked in this country, not always connecting that to particular policy decisions or
individual commitments by one party or the other, but just a desire to change things that ran
so strong that for some, the idea of just kind of burning it all down sounded better than trying
to have their lives improve with the status quo. And this is the thing that Democrats need to now
be paying attention to, because, you know, part of what was a trap for us in 2016, just as it was
in 2024, was that in our horror at the destruction of so many institutions of American life,
we became defenders of those institutions in ways that made it feel like we were defending a status
that frankly we didn't love that much either.
Now is the time to make clear we understand our task is not
to go back and find all the bits and the shards
of the status quo that have been smashed to pieces,
tape them back up together and give people some semblance
of what we used to have.
This is about making sure that we're prepared
for what's next and that we're very selective
about which norms, institutions, even agencies,
we really do need to put back together
and which ones need to be fully replaced
now that they've been destroyed.
So here's something that happened.
J.D. Vance, the vice president of the United States, the vice president for president who
was so clearly repudiated by the American electorate in so many states, issues a statement
on Twitter not only criticizing the war that the president single-handedly brought us into,
but also clearly or implicitly announcing himself as the candidate and putting a big
distance between himself and the president of the United States.
Are we off to the races?
It feels that way.
Look, we watched a lot of Republican candidates, mainly members of Congress, trying to find
some way to keep the Trump stink from attaching to them.
And in almost every case, they failed.
Now if you can't keep that stink off of you as a member of the Republican Party who may
be deep down wishes that Donald Trump never came to power, imagine how much harder it is
as somebody who has attached yourself, who shares the name of the administration, the
Trump Vance administration, a very difficult task to do, especially for somebody who is
still within that administration.
Let's be clear, J.D. Vance owns every bad decision of the Trump Vance administration from its
bad economic policies to its disastrous war in Iran.
And the fact that he deep down knows better, the fact that he originally compared Donald
Trump to Hitler before he got on board, doesn't make all of this better.
It makes all of this worse.
And you think he meant Hitler in a bad way?
I have to think he didn't mean it in a good way.
Exactly.
So you're on Fox almost as much as Sean Hannity.
And when you talk to those guys, do you get a sense from them that they know what's what?
No.
I was toggling the channels, watching how Fox was trying to make sense of this.
And what they didn't seem to be recognizing was that unpopular Republican policies led
to bad results and that voters are punishing Republican office holders for that.
I mean, it really is that simple.
Things like the tariffs and the tax cuts for the rich were unpopular.
They were supposed to be maybe unpopular things that you do anyway because they bring benefits
It's like more manufacturing jobs or more economic growth.
And instead they failed to do that as well.
So not only was it, it's not even an unpopular policy
that you have to do in order to get a good result.
Their unpopular policies led to bad results.
None of that seems to compute, at least as of today,
for the hosts and the commentators that I'm seeing on Fox.
They're almost treating this like a weather event
that there's just nothing they could have done about.
Hopefully the fact that this is not just a defeat,
but an absolutely overwhelming comprehensive,
thoroughgoing rejection of Trump and the Republican party.
Hopefully at some point that leads
to a little more introspection.
You see it happening online a little bit.
I don't know how long it'll take for that
to catch up to the Fox Newsroom.
Well, is there a chance that the Democratic party
could overinterpret this election victory
as comprehensive as it is, as stunning as it is?
Yeah, there are many ways that Democrats
could get this wrong.
For example, while pursuing the oversight agenda is very important, we need accountability,
we need standards in this country.
If for one second it appears that a democratic Congress is more interested in retribution
than putting money in people's pockets and getting them relief from these disastrous
economic policies, that's going to be a real problem, substantively and politically.
Then how do you solve the problem, the moral problem, the moral and political problem of
balancing the urge to impeach, for example, but also the desire to set a moral and political
standard of proper behavior.
If you want to fight corruption, all kinds of malfeasance and offense, how do you do
that and at the same time not fall into it being subject number one, two, and three in
Washington?
Well, our North Star is making the American people better off, improving everyday life,
making it all more affordable.
An accountability agenda could come at the expense of that,
but a smart accountability agenda
would actually be serving that,
because there's a direct relationship
between bad policy outcomes
and potential corruption in the administration.
I'm thinking of everything from the bridge between here
in Michigan and Canada that got delayed,
evidently because a Trump superback donor
got to Howard Lutnick to what happened
to the victims of fraudsters who have been pardoned
by President Trump and how all of that came about.
The ability for companies to get somehow,
get an exemption to put toxic chemicals in the air
or in the ground or get a pass on dangerous food
or drug products.
I mean, the list goes on and on and on
and there is potentially a relationship
between those bad policies that hurt people
and the corruption.
So I think when we're thinking about accountability,
the focus isn't on, you know,
which Trump official or relative to go after.
The focus is on which victims we can support because there are real victims of this, from
ICE abuses to victims of corruption.
But what are you telling me?
Are you against any impeachment hearings of any kind, whether it's against the president
or Pete Hexeth or...?
Yeah, I'm not very interested in impeachment, especially when it comes to the president.
I'm more interested in things that will illuminate the patterns of corruption, that will empower
the victims of abuses by this administration and that will establish their certain kind
of behaviors.
I would focus on the behaviors, not the people.
I mean, the people will be held accountable, but it's about behaviors that would be wrong
whether they were done by a Democrat, an independent or a Republican.
Because the other thing about this accountability agenda is if we get it right, just like the
popular economic policies, I believe, and they are a call back to things that most Americans
can agree on.
You know, if we get it wrong, this could be divisive.
If we get this right, it is unifying.
Because part of what success looks like for the country
is to get to a place where even people who supported this,
even people who are part of it,
are able to step back and be as horrified by it
as the rest of us.
I'm speaking with Pete Buttigieg.
We'll continue in just a moment.
This is the New Yorker Radio Hour.
Wired has always put a microscope
on the people, power, and forces shaping our world.
Uncanny Valley brings that same fearless reporting
straight to your feed.
Is Doge finally over?
Will AI actually democratize American healthcare?
Each week, wired journalists from across the newsroom
are gonna unpack where politics, technology,
and Silicon Valley collide.
From conversations with tech leaders across Silicon Valley,
internet fandom investigations,
and government crackdowns on rigged gambling,
we're taking you all over the news cycle,
going straight inside the priorities,
pressures and power plays, driving today's biggest decisions.
Uncanny Valley tackles the questions keeping you up at night and helps make
sense of the future taking shape right now.
Listen to new episodes every Thursday, wherever you get your podcasts.
Hi, I'm Nicole Phelps, Global Fashion News and Futures Director at Vogue and
co-host of the Run Through Podcast.
Each week on the show, our listeners get an all-access pass into the world of Vogue.
On Tuesdays, join me as I interview influential designers like Calvin Klein,
Rachel Scott, and Simone Bellotti.
On Thursdays, join Chloe Mao, head of editorial content
at Vogue US, and Choma Naughty,
British Vogue's head of editorial content,
as they explore fashion through the lens of culture
with guests like Doja Cat and Margot Robbie.
Listen and watch the run-through with Vogue
wherever you get your podcasts and Vogue's YouTube channel.
I'm Vincent Cunningham.
I'm Nomi Fry.
I'm Alex Schwartz, and we host Critics at Large
from The New Yorker.
Each week, we pick a starting point,
The new novel you can't stop thinking about,
the movie everybody's seeing this weekend,
and we kind of go galaxy brand with it.
Right, we take the ideas at the center of these things
and trace them across history, across mediums,
all to get to the bottom of why this particular text
is important right now in politics and culture
and also in your everyday life.
We go highbrow, we go lowbrow,
we go everything in between.
Food culture, the meme culture,
Charlie XCX to Tony Morrison.
K-pop to the Kennedys.
From horror movies to heated rivalry.
From the Oscars to the Met Gala.
The Golden Bachelor of Wuthering Heights.
Great expectations to desperate housewives.
That's what we're talking about over here.
We're having fun.
It's Critics Alarch from The New Yorker.
Every Thursday, wherever you get your podcasts.
This is The New Yorker Radio Hour.
I'm David Remnick, and I've been speaking today
with Pete Buttigieg.
The dust hasn't really settled
on this year's midterm elections
And the 2028 race for the presidency, of course, is about to begin.
There's a totally open field and no clear front runner.
It may be a very crowded race.
But Pete Buttigieg will likely be among the contenders.
He first ran for the presidency in 2019 when he was still the mayor of South Bend, Indiana.
He then served as transportation secretary under President Biden.
Buttigieg has kept his name out there partly by holding his own with political opponents,
often on Fox News or campaigning for Democrats in deep red states.
So are you already feeling, which is that inflation today is higher than it was on day
one?
They have done the exact opposite of what they promised.
Well, is it 9% in the five administration?
And you're right, it's not where the Fed wants to see it quite yet.
But it's much lower than that.
It was 3.0% on day one of this administration.
At the end.
At the end, yeah.
Again, it was 3.0%.
Right.
And now it's higher under Trump.
Yeah, it was 9% in the Biden administration and 3.1% at the beginning of the Trump administration,
where we agree.
But that high profile has come with a real cost.
Just months ago, somebody called in a fake report to Michigan authorities to the effect
that Buttigieg was a danger to his children.
The kids were temporarily separated from him until the matter was resolved.
I'll continue my conversation now with Pete Buttigieg.
I gotta tell you, politics has never been pretty,
but it's never been uglier.
You had this instance where you had the harrowing experience
of being swatted this summer,
and then child protective services
are falsely called on you and your husband.
And some people have been saying
that this election is absolutely characterized
by this kind of ugliness,
and that maybe the moral fever has broken with its results.
Are you as optimistic as all that?
It's much too soon to declare that,
but I do think it's encouraging that when we saw
that the politics go in these nasty
and sometimes sinister, even evil directions,
that was not rewarded.
And so I think that that's an important thing,
that it's clear that Americans were disgusted with that too.
It's not just that they didn't like tax cuts for the rich
and the war and the high gas prices and the Medicaid cuts.
It's that people are just sick of all the bullshit.
And that is, I know it sounds a little more broad or ethereal, more of a vibe thing than
a policy thing, but I sense it.
I sense it deeply from the dozens of states that I've been to on the campaign trail this
year.
And I hope that means we can turn the page, not just on a politician, but on a kind of
politics that the vast majority of us would be glad to see way into the rearview mirror.
Pete, I read Kamala Harris' memoir.
It's called 107 Days.
She talks about wanting to pick you as a running mate,
and then she says, quote,
it was too big a risk,
and she was clearly referring to your sexuality.
How did you feel when you read that,
and we're constantly posed with that question?
Were you offended?
Look, I just view it differently.
Obviously, I wouldn't run for president in 2020 if I
thought that the presidency and our electability depended on fitting various identity boxes.
And my experience in the past has been that the candidates who are the most competitive,
the candidates who are the most electable, are the ones who are the most compelling.
Sometimes I think primary voters have started to psych themselves out by trying to imagine
some hypothetical swing or conservative voter.
But I can tell you that somebody who won Iowa, my margin of victory coming from independent
voters and even Republicans crossing over to caucus with the Democrats there in Iowa,
it's not as simple as that.
It's different from that.
And I think that one thing that we're seeing, even as the dust is still settling on the
midterms, is that the candidates who did the best are not all the ones who have been considered
quote, unquote, low risk.
They're the ones who were rooted in their community, clear in their message, willing
to go everywhere and compelling to voters.
You've got a situation now where the democratic race will begin in South Carolina.
You struggled with black voters as a presidential candidate, and I think you got 2% of the black
vote in South Carolina in 2020.
If you run again, do you feel better equipped to get a much larger proportion of that vote
and why?
Yeah, certainly the proportion of the black vote that propelled me to reelection as mayor
of South Bend, for example, was very different from the outcome of the South Carolina presidential
primary. That's fair.
Partly because the first time that most black voters in South Carolina met me or heard of
me, I was showing up asking for their vote and competing against Joe Biden, who they
had known for decades and trusted deeply. I built a different relationship with communities
around the country now, for the most part, in a given community. The last time they've
seen me if I wasn't campaigning for a great Democrat, I was showing up delivering federal
funds to improve life in their community.
So, you know, whether it's South Carolina or any other state, I certainly have a different
relationship to various places in the country than I did before.
And you know, it's been really thrilling this last year, year and a half to be in communities,
including places where people thought Democrats had no business competing, doing my part to
help these amazing candidates who put those races on the map.
What role do you think the DSA has in the in the discussion and argument within the Democratic Party?
Yeah, I think that it's frankly something that's aroused a lot more media excitement relative to the role inside the party
I think the decisions that are going to be made about policy will begin converging on things that
Have two things in common
something that a vast majority of Americans agree on,
and that a totality or near totality of Democrats agree on.
At the very least, I think we could agree that we should start with those things,
because there's plenty of them.
Plenty of things that the vast majority of Americans have long-favored and still have not gotten done,
including very, very basic things like raising the minimum wage,
and maybe this time around indexing it to inflation,
so you don't have to go back to Congress every day.
We haven't done this since 2009,
which means real wages for a minimum wage worker
are one third lower than they were the last time that Congress touched it.
And raising it wouldn't just affect the small proportion of American workers
who actually make the federal minimum wage, but tens of millions who make more than that
and would benefit from that ripple effect. That's just one example of a policy that I think
every Democrat and most Americans, by some measures, even most Republicans, can get on
board with. Let's start there. You once said that the right will label Democrats crazy socialists,
no matter what policies you actually support. But now that the DSA is stronger, do you think that
these labels hurt the Democratic Party in some way? Because as you know, as a frequent guest on
Fox, this is a theme that's every five minutes you hear it.
Well, you don't want to generalize from a case of one. But one thing I'll say is that they leaned
very heavily on those labels to try to save themselves in this election and it had no effect.
So, you know, I think, look, we should always make sure that we are portrayed accurately.
And you know, when you see some position that no actual real live Democratic candidate has
advocated, but that shows up in some, you know, DSA website, and you see somebody trying
to say that every Democrat is for that.
Obviously, we need to push back on something like that that is inaccurate.
But I think these labels in many ways have been thrown around so aggressively that they
have less meaning than ever.
Presidencies tend historically to be defined by very few issues.
If a presidency is able to take on one, two, maybe three big issues and succeed in a legislative
sense or even in a rhetorical sense of leaving a permanent mark, that's considered a great
victory.
In Obama's case, there was obviously the historical first to being the first black president and
then obviously Obamacare and he could count obviously other issues.
But what would be the signature initiative if you were to run for president?
What would be your emphasis?
And if it wasn't you as a candidate, what would you like to see somebody else carry
as a banner?
Well, you know, I've spent the last year or so making the case for us to take big swings
on what's wrong with our political and economic system.
I'm a little fatigued with the consultant conventional wisdom that says, don't talk
about political reform because it's at the expense of the kitchen table, I believe that
of course we lead with the kitchen table.
And to do so responsibly means facing a political system that has kicked the legs out from under
the kitchen table.
The people in Missouri voted overwhelmingly to raise the minimum wage and deliver paid
family leave.
They did that on a ballot referendum.
And the next year, the legislators, their elected representatives in Missouri, voted
to override them and take it back.
And then those legislators by and large got to keep their jobs.
Why?
Because of gerrymandering.
So there's a direct connection between people struggling to put food on the table and these
basic flaws in our democratic system.
I believe that a great democratic movement and perhaps a future democratic president,
although this shouldn't have to require a Democrat, I think it will, will be able to
put these things together and find a way to put more money in your pocket and get politics
out of your face at the same time.
One of the stunning things about the results in the election, and maybe specifically in
Texas, was the repudiation of big money involvement, the richest man in the history of humanity.
Invested $200 million in the Texas race alone, and I think nearly $500 million overall, and
it came to nothing.
His great concern among Democrats specifically about the Supreme Court decision that equated
money in politics with speech.
Did we get that wrong?
Money in politics is still a huge problem.
And it's a problem in primaries,
probably more than anything,
but it's a problem in general elections too.
I'm thrilled that the efforts to throw hundreds
of millions of dollars into these races largely failed.
But that doesn't mean that it's irrelevant
and it doesn't diminish the importance
of getting money out of politics.
It's not just the electoral effect of these dollars.
It's the fact that many members of Congress spend a majority,
and I mean literally a majority of their working hours,
sitting on the phone asking people for checks,
one or 2,000 bucks at a time.
The fact that people think twice about saying what they believe
because they are worried about what will happen to them
if they, basically if they piss off the wrong industry super PAC.
So this remains a major problem.
It shapes policy outcomes no matter who wins a given election.
And it's something the American people hate and are frustrated with.
And we need to do something about it.
You know, a hundred years ago, Bill Clark, richest man in America, in some ways,
the, uh, the Elon Musk of his day, was one of the copper barons in Montana.
He stuffed pockets in the legislature to get himself a US Senate seat.
And that was the, the peak of the corruption of the copper kings.
and it led to a piece of legislation in Montana,
the Corrupt Practices Act, I think it was called,
that wound up standing as the law of the land
for 100 years in a model for campaign finance reform
and ethics law.
In fact, it lasted until it was finally struck down
by John Roberts Supreme Court.
But it tells you that there are seasons for this corruption
or this kind of influence of money to hit a peak
and then people respond and do something about it.
And sure enough, in that great tradition,
by bipartisan vote, the people in Montana
just passed an initiative called the Montana Plan
that will take effect, if I'm not mistaken,
as early as the beginning of next year,
saying that you can't use corporate money in this way.
I'm sure it'll be challenged in the courts,
but it is a really exciting development.
And I think a real barometer of Americans' frustration,
whether we're in conservative areas or liberal areas,
with the role the money has come to play.
Pete, you're a big reader of history, among other things.
And this era between 2016 and 2026,
or it extends to 2028, presumably,
how do you think it would be characterized
in American history?
And is there any period in American history
that it's comparable to in your mind?
Well, look, you can point to any moment
of any number of moments of change or upheaval.
Some people are even invoking reconstruction.
And I think there is a bit of a whiff of that
in terms of the political potential of this moment.
What I really think about is the mid-century moment
from the end of the depression
to coming out of World War II, the new deal,
in terms of how so many things that were set up
in that moment have been the norm for our entire lives,
from the UN Security Council,
to elements of the committee structure in Congress,
to the norm of the 40-hour work week,
to the physical layout of our cities
designed around the automobile.
So much of what we're doing now
is playing out in a framework that was set up for the way things looked in the middle
of the 20th century. And that's why a lot of these institutions were showing their age,
in some cases falling apart even before the Trump White House took a sledgehammer to them.
And what that means to me is sitting here in the 2020s, where we are in a world that
is very, very different on every axis from the importance and the role of a more assertive
of China and Russia to the onset of artificial intelligence
to the way that we move around our communities and cities,
to the way that information moves through the media.
We could be and should be building a government
and a set of institutions and a set of norms
and social patterns that are gonna make sense
for the rest of this century.
Because I think the late 2020s, early 2030s
might be remembered as one of those formative periods
whose results wind up standing for the next 60, 70, 80, 90 years.
Pete, when you're thinking about the possibility of running for president,
what goes into a decision like that?
I remember quoting Barack Obama long before he ran,
saying that there's an element of insanity proposing oneself
as the best possible person to be president in the country,
that you have to make this incredible leap of the imagination
both for yourself and for the country.
Tell me about what goes into that decision.
Yeah, every time I thought about running for any office
from when I decided not to run for Congress one time
to when I decided to seek the presidency in 2020's race,
every time it's based on a process
where I look at two things and line them up
next to each other.
One is what the moment calls for,
what the office calls for,
whether that office is mayor of South Bend
or the American presidency.
And the other thing I look at is,
what do I bring to the table?
And what do I bring to the table
that's different from the others?
Knowing that there are a lot of other people
who would compete.
And following that process,
several times led me to run through something,
including of course, mayor and president
and races that didn't go my way,
like chair of the DNC or Indiana State Treasurer.
And also following that exact same process
led me almost two years ago now
to take a look at the governor's race here in Michigan
and the Senate race here in Michigan
and decide even though those were offices
that I cared a lot about,
that it was not the right thing for me to run.
And the other thing, of course,
and it's a cliche to say it, but it's true.
We're all human beings and we have families.
And you sit with your family and you think about
what your family will go through
as a result of any decision you make.
And you've had a taste of that and it's not pretty.
Yeah, to put it mildly.
And, but look, there are some things,
including what my family went through this summer,
that we should all be able to agree are not normal
to be the price of public service.
They just can't be.
It can't be like that.
And one thing I hope that Americans can come
to our collective senses about,
and I sense this by the way in the reaction to what happened
that most of us can agree that having a family
be harmed that way is just unacceptable.
And you look at things like what Vivek Ramaswamy
tried to do to Amy Acton,
and you look at the disgust around that,
not just from Democrats, but really all around.
I really believe that we have a chance as a country
to show that we get however fierce and ferocious
and furious our politics can get,
that that cannot become a normal part of this process.
Pete Buttigieg, it's a pleasure always to talk with you.
Great to be with you, thanks for having me.
I spoke with Pete Buttigieg last week.
